newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Mexico City mayor-elect vows to keep a local focus.
newsitem.headline: Mexico City mayor-elect vows to keep a local focus.

text.p: Mexico City Mayor-elect Cuauhtemoc Cardenas on Monday called for national economic policies dedicated to raising living standards, but pledged to stick to municipal issues when he assumes office in December.

"As mayor of Mexico City, I'll be dealing with the problems of Mexico City," Cardenas told Reuters Financial Television. "The problems of the country, are the problems of the country, and that's for the members of my party and the congress to deal with."

Cardenas vowed to raise the living conditions of Mexico City inhabitants by improving security and public services such as the water supply and reducing air pollution. He said he would work toward better education and health care systems.

Cardenas, who won a landslide victory on July 6 in the capital's first direct election for mayor, said Mexico has made good progress in implementing reforms, but added that the government needed to raise the public's well-being, rather than just balance its macroeconomic indicators.

Cardenas, who traveled to New York to attend the U.N.'s International Conference on Governance for Sustainable Growth and Equity, told a panel that Mexico needed to review certain aspects of its economic agenda.

"We have to develop new economic policies that take into consideration ... the requirement that the national economy be distributed and opportunities for income be accessible on a fair and equitable basis," Cardenas said.
He called for governance that "renews its commitment and strives to improve the conditions of life for all and is not governing merely to balance macroeconomic indicators."

He said he saw potential conflict on many issues between his leftist Party for the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI). Those conflicts would not work themselves out into governance of the Mexico City, he said.

He said that he expected to work closely with Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, who earlier in July loosened the reins of power to allow Cardenas greater control over the selecting his own police chief and attorney general.

"I want to believe that we will develop a relationship of close collaboration," Cardenas said. "I want to believe that it is in the interest of both to advance progress in the solution of problems in Mexico City."
The president will set Mexico City's $5 billion budget during Cardenas' three-year term of office.
Cardenas said the July elections had proved free and fair in many, but not all parts, of the country, and that he expected Mexico to make progress expanding democratization around the country .
